newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU diplomats see little hope for Helms-Burton breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: EU diplomats see little hope for Helms-Burton breakthrough.

text.p: European Union diplomats see little hope of persuading Denmark not to veto a proposal to allow EU states to combat Washington's controversial anti-Cuba trade laws at Monday's General Affairs Council.

Officials preparing for the Luxembourg meeting of EU Foreign Ministers said on Friday that despite intensive diplomatic effort by the Commission and the Irish Presidency, they were resigned to a blocking law being vetoed.
"We have not given up hope, but given the strength of Copenhagen's convictions it is hard to foresee a change of heart," said one senior diplomat on Friday.

Denmark stunned the Commission and its EU partners earlier this week when it said concerns over national sovereignty would prevent it from approving laws to counter Washington's Helms-Burton Act, an amalgamation of years of anti-Cuba policy.
The Danish government is currently embroiled in a court case brought by a citizens' group that accuses it of handing too much sovereignty to the EU.

Copenhagen says it cannot go along with EU action based on a catch-all clause in the EU's founding treaties, which is regarded with suspicion by governments wary of ceding too much authority to the bloc.

Diplomats will instead concentrate their efforts on fine-tuning the blocking tactics -- particularly one section which would allow the EU to waive an obligation for European companies or individuals not to comply with the Act.
The Danish decision will not affect a case brought by the Commission, the EU's executive, against the United States at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Geneva.
A WTO panel is due to convene on November 20 to rule on EU complaints that the act -- and similar laws which seek to quash trade with Iran and Libya -- is extra-territorial.

The foreign ministers are due to discuss proposals that would allow countersuits to be brought anywhere in Europe against litigants who sue European companies or individuals for contravening the Helms-Burton Act.

Among other things the act allows naturalised Americans to take action in U.S. courts against "traffickers" -- foreign companies or individuals accused of gaining from investments made in property confiscated in Cuba since the 1959 Communist revolution.

The practical implications of the act have been suspended until January, ostensibly to give U.S. special envoy Stuart Eizenstat the opportunity to encourage Washington's allies to join efforts to isolate Havana but also to postpone the issue until after the U.S. presidential elections on November 5.

Although President Bill Clinton is known to privately oppose parts of the act, he was pressured into agreeing its passage in March after Cuba shot down two private U.S. light aircraft it said had repeatedly strayed into Cuban airspace.
Following outrage from the EU, Mexico and Canada, Clinton suspended part of the act, although he passed another section which bars executives of "traffickers" from entering the U.S.

Executives from Canadian mining conglomerate Sherritt International, among them EU nationals, have been barred from entering the United States. Washington is expected to name more companies it accuses of trafficking later this year.
The European Union is still studying proposals to bar U.S executives involved in litigation from the 15-nation bloc and has already begun compiling a "watchlist" of potential litigants.
